map.sentence: OpenAI and Anthropic each say an internal AI model found an algorithm that refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis, though Anthropic says its version beats brute force only above 10 to the power 10,000 variables and no person is known to have checked its Lean proof.
In a preprint that is not yet peer-reviewed, researchers report that the audio-visual chat models Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni scored only 51 to 52 AUROC ... 90.8 for audio and 80.8 for visual.

Hob, an MIT-licensed desktop app from Frigade, runs a file-handling AI agent on local models from Gemma 4 E4B Compact up to gpt-oss 120B on machines with at least 8 GB of RAM, and uses code guards to catch small models that claim work they never did.
OpenAI and Anthropic each say an internal AI model found an algorithm that refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis, or ETH, a central conjecture in computer science.
Both results are posted as preprints, not peer-reviewed papers.
map.note: Dossier-news section 5 ('Peer review: none for either paper'); uncited status label.

map.sentence: No person is known to have checked Anthropic's machine-checked proof.
ETH holds that, in the worst case, answering this for n variables takes time that grows exponentially with n.
map.note: 3-SAT definition preceding this is a plain-language definition of a technical term, not a sourced fact.

map.sentence: A literature search run by Claude found more than 800 papers with results that hold only if ETH, or a stronger hypothesis, is true.
Ryan Williams of MIT told TechCrunch that many ETH-dependent papers "will need to be revisited" if the labs' claims hold up.
map.note: Attribution to Williams and 'if the claims hold up' per factcheck.json round 1.

map.sentence: Both describe algorithms that run in subexponential time, meaning the running time grows more slowly than any exponential.
The previous record for a deterministic 3-SAT algorithm, O(1.328^n), was still exponential.
Anthropic says an internal Claude research model found the core algorithm on Oct 16, using 14 million output tokens "and no human input".
Researchers then helped improve the presentation.
OpenAI's preprint, "The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False," is dated Oct 17 and was revised Oct 25.
It comes from an unnamed internal model.
It was one of three big results OpenAI released, spanning "math, physics and computer science".
Anthropic's paper acknowledges OpenAI's claim as independent and concurrent.
TechCrunch reports that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge suggested OpenAI was basing its solutions on pre-existing work.
map.note: TechCrunch paraphrase about OpenAI's solutions generally; no quote marks per factcheck round 1; 'We could not find his original post' is from dossier Unverified section.

map.sentence: Anthropic says its Lean proofs rest only on Lean's three standard axioms and pass three checkers, including one built independently, called nanoda.
"At the time of writing no person is known to have checked it," the paper says.
The Lean proof also differs from the printed proof, and only AI models compared the two.
The README adds that "no machine checks that this file says what the paper says".
OpenAI's repository says its results are "at different stages of verification" and not all have Lean versions.
Anthropic says its result "does not bear on the P vs NP question directly" and yields no practical algorithms.
Its bound beats brute-force search, which tries every setting, only when n tops 10 to the power 10,000 on its test formulas.
map.note: Only the 10^10000 threshold quoted, per caveat; 'test formulas' = 3-CNF with m=5n clauses.

map.sentence: Brute force "is already impractical for n = 100," the paper notes.
Scientific American calls OpenAI's algorithm "just a tiny bit faster than exponential time".
Still, Williams told TechCrunch that every computer scientist "should probably put a little more weight on the plausibility of P = NP".
On encryption, Williams said OpenAI "checked, and they were reasonably confident" the result implied no breaks.
OpenAI's outside reviewers for the result are Williams, Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, with David Gross leading a physics group, according to Forklog, an AI-translated secondary report.
Forklog reports the researchers stressed their participation is not an endorsement, and that OpenAI said participation is voluntary and unpaid.
map.note: Paraphrased without quote marks per factcheck round 1.

map.sentence: Williams sees "two or three alien-looking parts" in OpenAI's proof.
"I don't think that OpenAI's algorithm could possibly be the best algorithm you can get," he said.
He and colleagues released an open letter asking scientists for feedback.
He had earlier called OpenAI's release of proofs a "DDOS attack on mathematicians".
Scientific American notes that the model behind OpenAI's proofs remains proprietary.
Audio-visual AI chat models did no better than a coin flip at spotting a few doctored seconds in long videos, a preprint posted to arXiv on Oct 24 reports.
Yet the evidence was sitting inside the same models.
The paper, which introduces a benchmark called AV-FABLE, is not yet peer-reviewed.
map.note: Status label from dossier-research ('arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed').

map.sentence: "A few manipulated seconds can change the meaning of an otherwise authentic video," the authors write.
A replaced sentence can change what someone seems to have said. An inserted sound can suggest an event that never happened.
Asked directly, they scored only 51 to 52 detection AUROC.
Those reached 90.8 AUROC on audio and 80.8 on visuals.
The evidence "is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs," the authors suggest.
It reads frozen Qwen3-Omni audio and visual features, with separate decoders that mark when each track was edited.
On test videos like its training data, it scored 96.04 detection AUROC and 91.30 AV-mAP.
A rival method, UMMAFormer, reached 84.76 AV-mAP on the same features.
NFSR's false-alarm rate stayed between 2.97% and 4.67%, close to its 5% budget.
AV-FABLE holds 16,650 pairs of videos, 33,300 in all and about 998 hours.
That stops a detector from cheating on file format: classifiers given only metadata reach at most 54.6 AUROC.
Videos run a median of 88 seconds, and edits cover a median of 9.45% of each fake.
The median edited event lasts about 9 seconds.
Footage comes from existing research datasets: ActivityNet, EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and HDTF.
Gemini 3.7 Flash, as the paper names it, picked a real event in each video and planned the edit. A second model checked that the edit could be done.
Two human reviewers checked all 22,153 events, and a third settled the 7.7% where they disagreed.
"A joint timeline can therefore reward a prediction for finding the right moment even when it identifies the wrong stream," the authors write.
A separate study, FakeParts, found they cut human detection accuracy by up to 26% compared with traditional deepfakes.
An earlier benchmark, TASLE, tackled AI-made segments hidden in long real videos, but only on the visual track.
map.note: Visual-only scope is stated in AV-FABLE full text (dossier section 4); cited per factcheck round 1.

map.sentence: AV-FABLE adds audio and uses held-out TASLE videos as one of its tests.
NFSR posted the top AV-mAP in all three tests on data unlike its training set.
These are the authors' own numbers on their own benchmark, with no outside replication.
map.note: Dossier-research status label and section 6 ('Self-built benchmark, self-proposed winner').

map.sentence: On unfamiliar data, finding visual edits "remains the main open problem," with visual overlap scores of 26.42 to 41.21.
Shrinking video to 360p cut visual localization from 53.1 to 10.9 mAP in one test.
The authors concede that "pipeline-specific cues cannot be fully excluded," so the detector may be learning traces left by the generators.
Explaining what changed is the hardest part, and models often misidentify the operation or target.
Deepfake-Eval-2024, by other researchers, found open-source detectors' AUC fell 50% for video and 48% for audio on deepfakes from the wild.
The dataset, code and weights are promised but not released. Where licenses restrict it, source media won't be shared; the release will offer annotations and reconstruction utilities instead.
The authors say they do not provide end-to-end pipelines "intended for impersonation, fraud, or other malicious uses".
The team is from Tsinghua University and Peking University, with corresponding authors Jun Zhou and Xiu Li.
Hob is a desktop app from Frigade that runs an AI agent for your files on your own machine, using local models through llama.cpp.
It is open source under the MIT license
with downloads for Mac, Windows and Linux.

Its developer, who posted it to Hacker News on Oct 26, says small models claimed tool results without calling the tools or got stuck in loops. So he spent "a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts".
Hob's site says it is backed by Y Combinator.
map.note: Moved from caveat paragraph to intro per editor round 1.

map.sentence: **8 GB.** That's the minimum RAM, and the Mac version needs Apple Silicon.
**Four model sizes.** The docs pair Gemma 4 E4B Compact with 8 GB Macs, E4B with 16 GB, 26B with 24 GB and up, and gpt-oss 120B with workstations.
map.note: 'Four' is a count of the tiers in the inv-3 quote.

map.sentence: **15 tokens a second.** Hob picks "the smartest one that stays above about 15 tokens a second with room for a decent context," the developer wrote.
**Zero telemetry.** "Chats and files stay on your machine, and there is no telemetry," the docs say, and folder changes need your approval and can be undone.
**3 times in a row.** A guard that checks whether files a reply names exist on disk, because "checking the files instead of the words works in any language"
sits beside a loop guard that cuts off a reply when a long passage repeats three times in a row.
We found no independent review of Hob, and the developer has published no benchmarks yet.
map.note: 'No independent review' is from dossier-invention Status line.

map.sentence: One Hacker News tester said, "The models are really dumb, mainly".
Another wrote, "there are a zillion of these".
The Windows build isn't yet signed with a Microsoft certificate, so Windows shows a warning.
The developer says each system gets its own sandbox tool, but we read only the Linux code.
map.note: 'Read only the Linux code' from dossier-invention Unverified.

map.sentence: It says that on older kernels without Landlock, "the code runs unlimited".

All three stories check what an AI did instead of what it said. Anthropic's Lean files, AV-FABLE's feature probes and Hob's disk checks each go around the model's own answer, and each check still awaits human or independent review.
map.note: Synthesis of cited claims above; from topics.json thread.
